title: A Boston ZIP code, "02134", becomes 2134 the moment anything parses it as a number
assumption: A ZIP code can be safely stored or parsed as an integer; it's 'just a number' after all.

input.description: A US ZIP code stored in a numeric database column, or passed through a spreadsheet import / schema that infers 'number' for a 5-digit-looking string.

what_goes_wrong: The leading zero silently disappears, turning a real, valid ZIP code into a 4-digit number that fails every later format check and no longer matches the original address.
why: A ZIP code is an identifier made of digit CHARACTERS, not a numeric quantity; there's no meaningful arithmetic anyone would do with it. int()/parseInt()/Number() all discard leading zeros because they parse decimal numeric VALUE, and the value of 02134 is mathematically identical to 2134 — the leading zero carries no numeric information, but it is semantically part of the identifier.
affects: any database column typed as an integer for a zip/postal code

repros.code:
zip_code = "02134"
as_int = int(zip_code)
print(as_int, str(as_int))
print(str(as_int) == zip_code)

fix: Store postal codes as strings, never as a numeric type, and never round-trip them through int()/parseInt()/Number() — there is nothing numeric about an identifier that happens to look like digits.

sources.title: Michael Tandy: Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Addresses

test_cases.note: Round-tripping a ZIP code through your storage layer should preserve the leading zero.
